[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This facility, Tahoe Reno 4, is part of Switchs Citadel Campus (Tahoe Reno) in Storey County, Nevada. Per Switchs own press release announcing the Tahoe Reno campus opening (tier-1 operator source, https://www.switch.com/switch-tahoe-reno-data-center-now-open/), this is the Citadel Campus, a 2,000 acre site in the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center in Storey County, Nevada, next to the Tesla Gigafactory, designed for up to 7.2 million square feet and up to 650 MW of power at full build out, a small fraction of which this registry currently tracks as five buildings. Aggregator directories (datacenterHawk, DataCenterMap) give 1 Superloop Circle, Reno, NV as the address for this campus, the same address appears attached to more than one individually numbered Tahoe Reno building on these directories, so it is treated here as a shared campus level address rather than a distinct address for any one building. Switch own official locations page (fetched directly this session, https://www.switch.com/locations/) names five exascale campuses, the Citadel in Tahoe Reno, the Pyramid Campus in Grand Rapids, the Core Campus in Las Vegas, the Keep Campus in Atlanta, and the Rock Campus in Austin and Houston, but confirms no street address for any campus or building, directing visitors to a contact form instead. This registry rows address, where given below, therefore comes from data center industry aggregator directories, leads-only sources per this projects source hierarchy, not confirmed directly by the operator.

reading.body:
Switch's Tahoe Reno 4 facility is one of five buildings currently tracked at the Citadel Campus, a 2,000 acre site in Storey County designed for up to 650 MW at full buildout, but this registry does not assign megawatts to individual buildings within it.

The Citadel Campus sits adjacent to Tesla's Gigafactory in an industrial zone optimized for power-intensive operations. Its scale, planned across multiple buildings rather than a single structure, reflects the economics of AI infrastructure: operators consolidate capacity at sites with available grid power and land. Switch's strategy of developing five exascale campuses across different US regions suggests a distribution model, moving compute closer to different power sources rather than concentrating it.

The data does not specify how much of the 650 MW target has been built or energized, nor does it reveal the actual power draw of Tahoe Reno 4 itself. It covers footprint and ambition, not the grid constraint that determines when and whether these buildings actually run at scale.
